title: Delirium: Acute Brain Failure Until the Cause Is Found
bottomLine: Acute fluctuating inattention and cognitive change is delirium until a precipitating medical, medication, withdrawal or environmental cause is found. Treat the cause, restore physiologic and sensory stability, and use nonpharmacologic safety strategies; sedatives and antipsychotics do not cure delirium.
recognize: Inattention, fluctuating alertness and disorganized thinking can be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed.
Hypoactive delirium is easily missed and may present as quiet withdrawal, reduced intake or slowed responses rather than agitation.
differentiate: Dementia is chronic/progressive and can coexist with delirium; depression can mimic cognitive impairment but does not usually cause acute fluctuating attention.
A positive urine culture without urinary/systemic infection does not automatically explain delirium.
assessment: Check oxygenation, glucose, infection, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, medications/anticholinergics/sedatives, withdrawal, sleep and sensory deficits.
Obtain collateral baseline cognition and function.
workup: Order targeted labs, urinalysis/culture only when UTI is clinically plausible, ECG/toxicology or imaging based on the syndrome.
Neuroimaging is not routine for every delirious older adult but is urgent with trauma, focal deficit or another intracranial concern.
management: Correct causes, mobilize, reorient, restore glasses/hearing aids, normalize sleep/wake cues, hydrate/nourish and minimize lines/restraints.
Use medication only for severe dangerous agitation when non-drug strategies fail and after reversible causes are addressed.
Alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal is a distinct setting where benzodiazepines may be appropriate.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics and polypharmacy commonly precipitate/worsen delirium.
Antipsychotics carry QT, stroke, movement and mortality risks and should not be routine chemical restraint.
counselling: Explain to family that delirium is a medical syndrome and recovery can lag after the trigger is treated.
followUp: Reassess cognition after recovery because delirium can unmask underlying neurocognitive disease; reconcile precipitating medications before discharge.
examTrap: Treating delirium with an antipsychotic before checking oxygen, glucose, retention, infection, medications and withdrawal.
oneLinePearl: Delirium is a cause-finding emergency, not a behaviour diagnosis.

title: Meningitis and Encephalitis: Stabilize and Treat Before the CSF Is Perfect
bottomLine: Fever with meningismus, altered mental status, seizure or rapidly progressive neurologic illness is a time-critical CNS infection syndrome. Obtain blood cultures and CSF when safe, but never allow CT or lumbar-puncture logistics to delay empiric antimicrobial therapy in a deteriorating patient with strong bacterial meningitis or encephalitis concern.
recognize: Bacterial meningitis may cause fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting or altered consciousness, but the classic triad is often incomplete.
Encephalitis is suggested by altered behaviour/consciousness, focal deficits or seizures with infectious/inflammatory features.
differentiate: Subarachnoid hemorrhage, severe migraine, sepsis-associated encephalopathy, toxic/metabolic disease and intracranial mass can mimic parts of the syndrome.
HSV encephalitis can present without classic meningismus and still requires urgent antiviral coverage when plausible.
assessment: Assess ABCs, GCS/mental status, seizure, focal deficit, rash, immune status, recent antibiotics, travel/exposure and age-specific risk.
workup: Obtain blood cultures and CSF cell count, glucose/protein, microbiology/PCR when LP is safe.
Use head imaging before LP selectively when features raise concern for mass effect/herniation rather than routinely delaying LP/treatment in every patient.
management: Start age/risk-appropriate empiric IV antimicrobials promptly and add acyclovir when encephalitis is plausible; use dexamethasone when indicated by the bacterial meningitis pathway.
Apply appropriate droplet precautions for suspected meningococcal disease and notify public health.
medicationSafety: Renal function matters for acyclovir and selected antimicrobials, but first doses should not be delayed for nonessential testing in a high-risk patient.
Tailor final therapy rapidly to CSF/blood microbiology and susceptibility.
counselling: Explain the urgency and public-health/contact implications when meningococcal disease is possible.
followUp: Ensure microbiology, contact prophylaxis/public-health actions and hearing/neurocognitive follow-up are closed-loop when indicated.
examTrap: Waiting for CT and lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics to a deteriorating patient with a convincing bacterial meningitis syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Diagnostics refine meningitis care; they must not create a treatment delay.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada meningococcal resources

title: Myasthenia Gravis: Fatigable Weakness With a Respiratory Safety Net
bottomLine: Myasthenia gravis causes fluctuating fatigable skeletal-muscle weakness, often ocular/bulbar, without sensory loss. Confirm autoimmune neuromuscular-junction disease, screen for thymic disease, use symptomatic and immunomodulatory therapy through neurology, and treat respiratory/bulbar deterioration as potential myasthenic crisis rather than waiting for oxygen saturation to fall.
recognize: Ptosis/diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, neck/proximal weakness and worsening with repeated activity are classic.
Sensation and pupils are usually preserved; reflexes are generally preserved, which helps separate other neuromuscular disorders.
differentiate: Lambert-Eaton often improves transiently with exercise and may have autonomic symptoms/reduced reflexes; botulism includes autonomic/pupillary findings; brainstem stroke is usually abrupt and not characteristically fatigable.
Medication toxicity, infection and physiologic stress can precipitate worsening.
assessment: Assess ocular/bulbar symptoms, secretion handling, cough strength, respiratory effort, neck/proximal power and medication/infection triggers.
Do not rely on pulse oximetry to exclude impending ventilatory failure.
workup: Use AChR/MuSK and other antibody testing plus electrodiagnostic testing when appropriate; chest imaging evaluates thymoma/thymic disease.
In significant respiratory/bulbar weakness, serial bedside respiratory measurements and critical-care assessment are more important than waiting for confirmatory outpatient tests.
management: Pyridostigmine can improve symptoms; corticosteroid/steroid-sparing immunotherapy and thymectomy decisions are individualized through neurology.
Myasthenic crisis requires monitored respiratory support and rapid immunomodulatory treatment such as IVIG or plasma exchange under specialty/critical care.
medicationSafety: Magnesium, aminoglycosides, selected fluoroquinolones/macrolides, beta-blockers and other drugs can worsen neuromuscular transmission in susceptible patients; review necessity and alternatives.
Excess cholinesterase inhibitor can also cause weakness with cholinergic symptoms; do not reflexively increase dose during unexplained deterioration.
counselling: Teach medication-trigger awareness, infection planning and that new swallowing/breathing weakness requires urgent assessment.
followUp: Track function, respiratory/bulbar symptoms and immunotherapy toxicity with neuromuscular specialty care.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with worsening bulbar weakness because SpO2 is still normal.
oneLinePearl: Myasthenic respiratory failure is a ventilation problem—oxygen saturation can stay normal until late.

title: Bell Palsy: Protect the Eye After Excluding a Broader Neurologic Syndrome
bottomLine: Bell palsy is an acute peripheral seventh-nerve palsy involving the forehead and lower face after stroke, zoster, Lyme disease and structural/recurrent causes are reasonably excluded. Early corticosteroid therapy is useful in appropriate patients, but corneal protection is the immediate safety priority when eye closure is incomplete.
recognize: Complete unilateral facial weakness including forehead, impaired eye closure, altered taste, hyperacusis or retroauricular discomfort can occur.
Symptoms typically develop over hours to a few days rather than as a slowly progressive mass lesion.
differentiate: Forehead sparing with other focal deficits suggests a central lesion; vesicular ear pain suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome; recurrent, bilateral or progressive palsy requires broader evaluation.
Lyme exposure/geography and systemic clues change testing/treatment considerations.
assessment: Perform full neurologic and ear/skin exam, assess eye closure/corneal symptoms, hearing/vestibular symptoms, Lyme risk, pregnancy/diabetes and other cranial nerves.
workup: Routine imaging is not required for a classic isolated presentation; investigate atypical, recurrent, progressive or multi-cranial-nerve disease.
Use Lyme or other testing when exposure/clinical context warrants it.
management: Start corticosteroid early when appropriate; use lubricating drops/ointment and eyelid-taping or ophthalmic strategies to prevent corneal injury.
Add antiviral therapy selectively when severe palsy/zoster features or current guideline indications apply.
medicationSafety: Review glucose effects of corticosteroids and pregnancy context.
Do not delay eye protection while waiting for diagnostic testing.
counselling: Teach meticulous eye care and expected recovery trajectory; advise reassessment if new neurologic symptoms emerge.
followUp: Reassess incomplete recovery and refer atypical/prolonged cases to neurology/ENT/ophthalmology as indicated.
examTrap: Diagnosing Bell palsy from facial droop without testing forehead movement and the rest of the neurologic examination.
oneLinePearl: Bell palsy is isolated peripheral CN VII weakness; anything more deserves another diagnosis.

title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Median-Nerve Pattern Before Testing
bottomLine: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median-nerve compression at the wrist diagnosed from a characteristic sensory/motor pattern plus examination. Electrodiagnostic or ultrasound testing is most useful when diagnosis is uncertain, severity/surgery needs clarification, or another neuropathy is plausible—not as a prerequisite for every classic mild case.
recognize: Nocturnal numbness/tingling in thumb-index-middle/radial ring fingers, hand shaking for relief and thenar weakness in advanced disease are typical.
Symptoms may worsen in pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism or repetitive wrist exposure.
differentiate: C6/C7 radiculopathy, ulnar neuropathy, polyneuropathy and thumb arthritis can mimic hand symptoms.
Persistent thenar atrophy/weakness suggests more severe nerve injury than intermittent paresthesia alone.
assessment: Map sensory distribution, thenar strength/atrophy, provocative wrist maneuvers, neck symptoms and other nerve distributions; assess occupational/pregnancy/medical contributors.
workup: Use electrodiagnostic testing or neuromuscular ultrasound when confirmation/severity matters, before surgery when required, or when the pattern is atypical/multifocal.
Do not order cervical MRI simply because hand tingling exists without a cervical/root pattern.
management: Use neutral-position night splinting and activity/ergonomic modification for many mild-moderate cases; corticosteroid injection can provide relief in selected patients.
Persistent sensory loss, thenar weakness/atrophy or failure of conservative therapy warrants surgical referral; carpal tunnel release is highly effective when appropriately indicated.
medicationSafety: Avoid relying on chronic opioids or sedating analgesics for nerve compression that needs mechanical treatment.
Injection risks and pregnancy/diabetes context should be reviewed individually.
counselling: Teach night splint positioning and that worsening weakness—not just pain—changes referral urgency.
followUp: Track sensory symptoms and strength; escalate if function declines despite conservative care.
examTrap: Ordering extensive cervical imaging before confirming that the symptoms fit a median-nerve wrist distribution.
oneLinePearl: CTS is a median-nerve pattern first; testing answers uncertainty and severity.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Physical Medicine/Rehabilitation and related CTS evidence

title: Lumbar Radiculopathy: Root Symptoms Without Reflex MRI
bottomLine: Lumbar radiculopathy is a nerve-root syndrome defined clinically by radiating pain plus neurologic/root findings. In the absence of cauda equina, infection, cancer, fracture or severe/progressive deficit, early MRI usually does not improve care; start evidence-based conservative treatment and image when red flags, persistent disabling symptoms or procedural/surgical planning make the result actionable.
recognize: Dermatomal leg pain, paresthesia, myotomal weakness and reflex changes support radiculopathy.
Positive nerve-tension maneuvers can support the diagnosis but are not sufficient alone.
differentiate: Peripheral neuropathy, hip pathology, vascular claudication and nonspecific referred back pain can mimic radicular symptoms.
Cauda equina syndrome adds bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle anesthesia and/or severe multiroot deficits and is an emergency.
assessment: Assess motor strength, reflexes, dermatomal sensation, gait, bowel/bladder/saddle symptoms, fever, cancer, trauma, immunosuppression and osteoporosis.
workup: No routine imaging is needed initially for uncomplicated radiculopathy.

Urgent MRI is indicated for cauda equina, epidural infection/hematoma, severe/progressive deficit or other serious pathology; delayed MRI is reasonable when symptoms persist and surgery/injection is being considered.
management: Encourage activity as tolerated, targeted exercise/physiotherapy and appropriate nonopioid analgesia; avoid prolonged bed rest.
Refer severe/progressive weakness or persistent disabling symptoms with concordant imaging for spine specialty consideration.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine long-term opioids and cumulative sedating drugs; NSAIDs require GI/renal/CV risk review.
Gabapentinoids have limited benefit for many radicular pain presentations and can cause sedation/dizziness.
counselling: Explain that early imaging often finds incidental disc disease and does not necessarily speed recovery; teach red-flag return symptoms.
followUp: Reassess neurologic function and trajectory; persistent severe symptoms beyond conservative care may justify imaging/referral.
examTrap: Ordering immediate lumbar MRI for uncomplicated sciatica with stable strength and no red flags.
oneLinePearl: Radiculopathy earns a neurologic exam first; MRI comes when the result will change management.

title: Cervical Radiculopathy: Separate a Nerve Root From the Spinal Cord
bottomLine: Cervical radiculopathy causes arm pain/sensory/motor/reflex findings in a root pattern, but upper-motor-neuron signs, gait dysfunction or bowel/bladder symptoms suggest cervical myelopathy and require urgent imaging/specialty assessment. Uncomplicated stable radiculopathy can begin with conservative care before MRI.
recognize: Neck/arm pain with dermatomal sensory symptoms, myotomal weakness and reduced reflexes support radiculopathy.
Hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, gait imbalance, pathologic reflexes or broad bilateral symptoms suggest cord involvement rather than isolated root disease.
differentiate: Shoulder disease, carpal/ulnar neuropathy, brachial plexopathy and cardiac referred pain can mimic cervical radiculopathy.
Cervical myelopathy is a different urgency and must not be managed as routine radicular pain.
assessment: Map myotomes/dermatomes/reflexes, examine gait and upper-motor-neuron signs, assess shoulder/peripheral nerve alternatives and screen trauma/cancer/infection risk.
workup: MRI is urgent for myelopathy or progressive deficit and appropriate when persistent symptoms are severe enough to consider procedure/surgery.
Electrodiagnostics may help when peripheral entrapment vs radiculopathy remains unclear.
management: Use activity modification, physiotherapy/exercise and appropriate analgesia for stable uncomplicated disease.
Urgently refer myelopathy, significant progressive weakness or suspected serious structural disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged high-risk analgesic/sedative regimens when mechanical/neurologic reassessment is needed.
Cervical manipulation is inappropriate when instability, myelopathy or other high-risk pathology is suspected.
counselling: Teach the difference between arm pain that can be monitored and new gait/hand/bowel/bladder changes that need urgent reassessment.
followUp: Reassess strength/reflexes/function; image/refer if deficits progress or conservative care fails.
examTrap: Treating hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia and gait imbalance as simple cervical radiculopathy.
oneLinePearl: A root causes LMN-pattern arm findings; a cord changes gait, reflexes and urgency.

title: Vertigo and Dizziness: Timing, Triggers, Exam, Then Location
bottomLine: Do not diagnose dizziness from adjectives alone. Use timing, triggers, eye movements, gait and focal neurologic findings to separate benign positional/peripheral syndromes from posterior-circulation stroke, presyncope, arrhythmia and metabolic disease; non-positional vertigo with brainstem/cerebellar features needs urgent neurovascular assessment.
recognize: BPPV causes brief triggered positional episodes with characteristic positional nystagmus.
Vestibular neuritis causes continuous acute vestibular syndrome without hearing loss; labyrinthitis adds auditory symptoms.
Posterior stroke can present with vertigo/ataxia and may lack obvious limb weakness.
differentiate: Presyncope/lightheadedness requires cardiovascular/orthostatic evaluation rather than a vestibular label.
HINTS is useful only in the correct continuous acute vestibular syndrome and when performed/interpreted by a trained clinician; misuse can falsely reassure.
assessment: Characterize timing/triggers, hearing loss, severe headache/neck pain, vascular risk, chest symptoms and neurologic symptoms; examine gait, cranial nerves, nystagmus/eye movements and orthostatic vitals when appropriate.
workup: Typical BPPV generally requires no imaging or specialized vestibular testing.

Urgent stroke-capable neurovascular imaging is indicated when central/brainstem/cerebellar features or high-risk posterior-circulation syndrome are present; CT can be insensitive for posterior fossa ischemia.
management: Treat confirmed BPPV with canalith repositioning rather than chronic vestibular suppressants.
Use short-term antiemetic/vestibular-suppressant therapy selectively for severe peripheral symptoms; prolonged use can delay compensation.
Central suspicion belongs on the stroke pathway.
medicationSafety: Sedating vestibular suppressants increase falls/delirium risk, particularly in older adults.
Do not assume dizziness after a medication change is benign without checking BP, rhythm, glucose and neurologic status.
counselling: Teach safe positional manoeuvres when appropriate, fall precautions and which new neurologic symptoms require emergency care.
followUp: Persistent/atypical symptoms need diagnostic reconsideration rather than indefinite vestibular-suppressant refills.
examTrap: Calling all spinning dizziness BPPV and prescribing meclizine/dimenhydrinate without checking gait or neurologic findings.
oneLinePearl: Timing plus triggers plus neurologic exam beats the word 'dizzy'.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices posterior-circulation/TIA guidance
